message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative, so H⁻ is unstable in free space) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Atomic radius | ~31 pm (covalent) |
| | Van der Waals radius | ~120 pm |
| **Physical State at STP** | State | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (−423.17 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (−434.69 °F) |
| | Density (gas) | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat capacity (gas) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at constant pressure) |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.449 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Heat of fusion | 0.000 kJ mol⁻¹ (negligible) |
| | Thermal conductivity | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Electrical conductivity | Very low (non‑metallic) |
| | Refractive index | 1.000132 (visible light) |
| | Speed of sound | ~1270 m s⁻¹ (in pure H₂) |
| **Chemical Properties** | Oxidation states | +1 (as H⁺), –1 (as H⁻) |
| | Bonding | Forms covalent bonds; H₂ is diatomic with a single σ bond |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive; forms hydrides with metals, acids with nonmetals |
| | Combustion | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, releases ~286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (H⁺ donor) or base (H⁻ acceptor) depending on context |
| | Solubility | Insoluble in water (~0.0006 g 100 mL at 25 °C) |
| | Spectral lines | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) |
| | Ionization potential | 13.598 eV (first) |
| | Dissociation energy (H₂) | 4.478 eV (≈432 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Bond length (H₂) | 0.741 Å |
| | Dipole moment | 0 (homonuclear diatomic) |
| | Magnetic moment | 1 µB (electron spin) |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Most abundant (99.98 %) |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable isotope, heavier, used in heavy water (D₂O) |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β⁻ emitter, half‑life ≈12.32 y) |
| | Isotope effects | Deuterium forms stronger bonds (e.g., D₂O has higher boiling point) |
| **Applications & Significance** | Energy carrier | Hydrogen fuel cells, rocket propellant |
| | Industrial uses | Production of ammonia (Haber process), methanol, hydrogenation reactions |
| | Environmental impact | Clean combustion (water only) but requires renewable production for sustainability |
| | Astrophysical relevance | Most abundant element in the universe; key in stellar nucleosynthesis |
| | Safety considerations | Extremely flammable; forms explosive mixtures with air (1–4 % H₂ in air) |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element in the universe.
- **Highly reactive**: It readily forms compounds with almost all other elements.
- **Energy potential**: As a clean-burning fuel, it’s central to future energy strategies, though its production must be green to avoid CO₂ emissions.
- **Isotopic diversity**: The presence of stable deuterium and radioactive tritium adds unique chemical and physical nuances.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
